name: supply_demand
description: A price–quantity market diagram: downward-sloping demand, upward-sloping supply, equilibrium where they cross. Choose this scene for ANY request about markets, demand/supply, equilibrium, price ceilings or floors (shortage/surplus), taxes, subsidies and deadweight loss, consumer/producer surplus, or curve shifts. All geometry is computed for you — you only choose which ingredients to include. Spec-level region elements can shade between this scene's curves (between: [supply_curve, demand_curve], or a price line like ceiling_line) — e.g. to shade a shortage wedge or a surplus area not covered by the built-in regions.

steepness.description: Either a word (gentle=0.55, medium=1, steep=1.5) or a numeric factor k. Use a number when the value must animate, and give it a number in the base params too — an animate with no numeric start jumps straight to the target. The visible range ENDS at k ≈ 1.05, where the shape clips to the plot: every value above that draws the SAME curve, so `steep` ≈ `medium`. To make one curve read as markedly steeper, flatten the other instead.

elasticity.description: How flat or steep the curve is, as an elasticity — the lever to use for tax incidence. Words: perfectly_inelastic (0.06), inelastic (0.5), unit (1, default), elastic (1.5), perfectly_elastic (1.94); or any number in that range, which animates. Unlike steepness, which saturates, this reaches near-vertical and near-horizontal. Changing it never moves the equilibrium, so two figures at different elasticities are directly comparable.

supply.description: The supply curve. Set to null to draw demand only.

steepness.description: Either a word (gentle=0.55, medium=1, steep=1.5) or a numeric factor k. Use a number when the value must animate, and give it a number in the base params too — an animate with no numeric start jumps straight to the target. The visible range ENDS at k ≈ 1.05, where the shape clips to the plot: every value above that draws the SAME curve, so `steep` ≈ `medium`. To make one curve read as markedly steeper, flatten the other instead.

elasticity.description: Same as demand.elasticity, applied to supply.

equilibrium.description: Equilibrium marker where D and S cross (shown by default when both curves exist).

guides.description: Dashed guide lines to both axes (default true).

q_label.description: Label on the quantity axis, default "Q*".

p_label.description: Label on the price axis, default "P*".

demand_shift.description: A shifted demand curve D→D′ with a shift arrow. When both demand_shift and supply_shift are set, no new (shifted) equilibrium is drawn — v1 limit.

direction.description: Fallback used only when amount is not set (right = +15, left = -15).

amount.description: Signed horizontal shift in domain units (0–100 axis). When set, wins over direction. 0 is legal: the shifted curve coincides exactly with the base curve — the canonical animate start state. Positive = right, negative = left.

arrow.description: horizontal (default): same price, more (less) wanted or offered. vertical: same quantity, a higher (lower) price. perpendicular: square to the old curve.

supply_shift.description: A shifted supply curve S→S′ with a shift arrow. When both demand_shift and supply_shift are set, no new (shifted) equilibrium is drawn — v1 limit.

direction.description: Fallback used only when amount is not set (right = +15, left = -15).

amount.description: Signed horizontal shift in domain units (0–100 axis). When set, wins over direction. 0 is legal: the shifted curve coincides exactly with the base curve — the canonical animate start state. Positive = right, negative = left.

arrow.description: horizontal (default): same price, more (less) wanted or offered. vertical: same quantity, a higher (lower) price. perpendicular: square to the old curve.

numbering.description: prime (default): D, E, P*, Q* → D′, E′, P*′, Q*′. index: D₁, E₁, P₁, Q₁ → D₂, E₂, P₂, Q₂ — textbook form, counts on for further changes.

tax.description: A tax on the market: draws the shifted curve, the new equilibrium, and the two prices the two sides now face — the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive. Use for any request about tax incidence, who bears a tax, tax revenue, subsidies, or deadweight loss from a tax. Nothing is SHADED unless you also list it in `regions`.

amount.description: Size of the tax in price-axis units — the axis runs 0-100 and the untaxed equilibrium sits at 50, so 18 is a substantial tax and the default for kind per_unit. NEGATIVE IS A SUBSIDY: the curve shifts the other way, more is traded, and `government_revenue` becomes a government cost. Numeric, so it animates: tween it from 0 to watch the wedge open and the deadweight loss grow. For kind ad_valorem this is a PERCENTAGE instead, default 36 (36%).

side.description: Who the tax is collected from: seller (default) shifts supply up, buyer shifts demand down. The figure comes out IDENTICAL either way — same quantity, same two prices — which is the point worth showing when a request asks whether it matters who pays.

kind.description: per_unit (default) is a fixed amount per unit, so the curve shifts parallel. ad_valorem is a percentage of the price, so the curve PIVOTS from the origin and the wedge widens as price rises — the realistic shape for VAT or sales tax.

label.description: Default "S + tax", or "D - tax" for a buyer-side tax.

price_ceiling.description: A price ceiling on the market; when it binds below equilibrium (see `level`) also shows the resulting shortage (Qd > Qs) by default.

level.description: Where the line sits, in price-axis units (same 0-100 scale as tax.amount). Sliding it down opens the shortage and grows the deadweight loss in one gesture. A ceiling only BINDS below the equilibrium price; above it the line is drawn and nothing else happens, which is a legitimate figure about a ceiling that does nothing.

price_floor.description: A price floor on the market; when it binds above equilibrium (see `level`) also shows the resulting surplus by default.

level.description: Where the line sits, in price-axis units (same 0-100 scale as tax.amount). Sliding it up opens the surplus and grows the deadweight loss in one gesture. A floor only BINDS above the equilibrium price; below it the line is drawn and nothing else happens, which is a legitimate figure about a floor that does nothing.

regions.description: Which areas to shade. NOTHING IS SHADED UNLESS LISTED HERE — ask for an area on the beat that explains it, not by default. Every area is computed against whichever intervention is set (tax, ceiling or floor), not against the untaxed market: with a tax, consumer surplus is measured from the price buyers actually pay. government_revenue is the tax wedge (a government COST when the amount is negative) and is skipped for a price control, where both sides face one price; transfer is the surplus a price control moves between the two sides, and is skipped for a tax. A binding ceiling's consumer surplus assumes efficient rationing — the buyers who value the good most are the ones who get it.

element_ids.supply_curve: the supply curve (when supply is not null)
element_ids.guide_lines: dashed guides from the equilibrium to both axes
element_ids.demand_shift_curve / supply_shift_curve: the shifted curve (when a shift is set)
element_ids.demand_shift_arrow / supply_shift_arrow: arrow from the old to the new curve (see `arrow`); no arrowhead when |amount| < 2
element_ids.shift_equilibrium_point: dot at the new D–S crossing after a single shift (absent if both demand_shift and supply_shift are set)
element_ids.shift_guide_lines: dashed guides from the shifted equilibrium to both axes
element_ids.label_P_shift: price-axis label at the shifted equilibrium ("P*′" / "P₂")
element_ids.label_Q_shift: quantity-axis label at the shifted equilibrium ("Q*′" / "Q₂")
element_ids.tax_supply_curve / tax_demand_curve: the shifted curve — S+tax for a seller-side tax, D−tax for a buyer-side tax
element_ids.tax_guide_lines: dashed guides at the with-tax equilibrium
element_ids.price_buyers_point / price_sellers_point: dot at the price buyers pay (P_b) or sellers receive (P_s) — a tax only
element_ids.dwl_region: shaded deadweight-loss triangle — only when "deadweight_loss" is listed in `regions`; drawing it without that draws nothing at all
element_ids.wedge_region: shaded government-revenue wedge between P_b and P_s — a tax only, AND only when "government_revenue" is listed in `regions`; drawing it without that draws nothing at all
element_ids.transfer_region: shaded transfer between consumers and producers — a price control only, AND only when "transfer" is listed in `regions`; drawing it without that draws nothing at all
element_ids.shortage_guide_qd / surplus_guide_qd: dashed guide at the quantity demanded at the controlled price
element_ids.shortage_guide_qs / surplus_guide_qs: the same at the quantity supplied
element_ids.label_Qd / label_Qs: "Qd" / "Qs" under each guide — draw each with its guide, one beat each, before the gap
element_ids.cs_region / ps_region: shaded consumer/producer surplus — only when "consumer_surplus" / "producer_surplus" is listed in `regions`; drawing either without that draws nothing at all

examples.request: Draw a demand and supply diagram.
Show why a price ceiling creates a shortage.
Show demand increasing and where the new equilibrium lands.
Show that when demand is inelastic, buyers pay most of a tax.
What does a price ceiling cost society?
